clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive surfactant disorder caused by biallelic mutations in the ABCA3 lipid-transporter gene
It is one of the more common genetic causes of surfactant dysfunction and can mimic surfactant protein B deficiency in neonates
Severe biallelic loss of function causes fatal neonatal respiratory failure; milder alleles cause childhood interstitial lung disease
Electron microscopy classically shows small, abnormal lamellar bodies with dense inclusions
Chest imaging shows a diffuse ground-glass pattern, later with cysts or fibrosis in survivors
Response to exogenous surfactant is typically poor, as in other intrinsic surfactant disorders
Diagnosis is confirmed by genetic testing, supported by histology and electron microscopy
reference.pathophysiology: ABCA3 is a lipid transporter located in the limiting membrane of lamellar bodies within alveolar type II cells, where it is required for the transport of phospholipids into these surfactant storage organelles. Loss of ABCA3 function impairs lamellar body formation and surfactant lipid packaging, producing dysfunctional surfactant, characteristic small malformed lamellar bodies and type II cell injury. The severity depends on the residual transporter activity, so complete loss causes lethal neonatal disease while partial function produces a chronic interstitial lung disease phenotype.
additionalDifferentials: Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome of prematurity
Other childhood interstitial lung disease entities
Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis of other cause
additionalInvestigations: Lung biopsy with electron microscopy showing abnormal lamellar bodies
Immunostaining for surfactant proteins to exclude related disorders
Exclusion of infection and cardiac disease
redFlags: Severe neonatal respiratory failure without another explanation
Progressive hypoxaemia and increasing respiratory support
Family history of unexplained neonatal or childhood lung disease
reference.prognosis: Complete loss-of-function disease is often fatal in infancy without lung transplantation; partial-function variants cause chronic interstitial lung disease with a variable, sometimes protracted, course.
pitfalls: Attributing term-neonate respiratory failure only to infection or transient causes
Assuming a poor surfactant response rules out a surfactant disorder
Not pursuing electron microscopy or genetics in unexplained diffuse lung disease
Overlooking milder ABCA3 disease in older children with interstitial lung disease
references: Kendig's Disorders of the Respiratory Tract in Children (standard reference)
management: Provide supportive respiratory care as the foundation, with supplemental oxygen and mechanical ventilation for neonatal respiratory failure titrated to the severity phenotype
Trial empirical anti-inflammatory therapy in childhood interstitial lung disease with systemic corticosteroids, adding hydroxychloroquine and/or azithromycin, recognising that responses are variable
Optimise nutrition and growth and prevent respiratory infection with immunisations including RSV prophylaxis and prompt treatment of intercurrent infection
Recognise that exogenous surfactant replacement gives at best transient benefit in this intrinsic surfactant disorder
Refer severe or progressive disease for lung transplantation, the only definitive option for lethal loss-of-function disease
Offer genetic counselling and family testing for this autosomal recessive disorder, including reproductive-genetics advice
Manage within a specialist paediatric respiratory or neonatal multidisciplinary team
